purpose: Deterministic interoperability fixture. Each side implements the protocol independently and proves byte-for-byte agreement against these vectors. This file is the interoperability source of truth; neither repository depends on the other's runtime code.
secret_warning: The secret below is fictional and exists only to make these vectors reproducible. It must never be provisioned in any environment. Key ids here are illustrative.

signing_string_lines: 1. protocol version tag, the literal LegacyServiceAuth-v1
2. key id, exactly as sent in x-guos-key-id
4. request path, raw received bytes, percent-encoding preserved, no normalization
5. canonical query (empty string when there is no query string)
6. timestamp, exactly as sent in x-guos-timestamp
7. body SHA-256, lowercase hex, over the exact raw body bytes

canonical_query_rule: Split the raw query string on '&'; drop zero-length segments; keep every remaining segment verbatim including its original percent-encoding and its '=' if present; sort the segments in ascending order of their unsigned byte values, comparing byte by byte, with a proper prefix sorting first; join with '&'. Segments are never decoded, because percent-decoding is lossy ('+' versus '%20') and would not be reproducible across languages.
query_alphabet_rule: Every byte of the query must be printable ASCII, 0x21 to 0x7E, and a request carrying anything else is rejected before canonicalization. RFC 3986 already restricts the request target to ASCII, so this costs nothing, and it is what makes 'byte order' unambiguous across languages: under it a UTF-8 bytewise sort, a Python str sort and a JavaScript UTF-16 code-unit sort are the same ordering. Without it they are not, because UTF-16 encodes supplementary characters as surrogates in D800-DFFF, which sort below the BMP characters in E000-FFFF that UTF-8 encodes with a smaller lead byte. Implementations may therefore use their language's default string sort once this precondition is enforced.

header_grammar.note: Normative grammar, transcribed from ADR-111 section 2. It lives in a fenced block there, not a table, because a Markdown table cell requires '|' to be escaped as '\|' -- so an alternation renders as one thing and reads in source as another. An earlier draft carried exactly that defect here: '^(0\|[1-9][0-9]{0,11})$' matches no ordinary epoch at all, including this fixture's.

vectors.covers: C1 event ingestion: POST with a body and no query string.
C6 bounded read: GET with an empty body and a query string whose received order differs from canonical order, so a signer that forgets to sort cannot pass.

how_to_use.signer_side: Build the signing string from your own request, then assert it equals signing_string_base64 for the matching vector before comparing signatures. Comparing the signing string first is what localizes a canonicalization bug; comparing only the signature tells you it is wrong but not where.
how_to_use.verifier_side: Feed the vector's method, path, raw_query, timestamp and base64-decoded body through your verifier with the fictional secret bound to the vector's key id, and assert it accepts. Then mutate one field at a time and assert it rejects.
how_to_use.negative_cases: ADR-111 section 'Contract tests' enumerates the rejection cases both sides must cover. They are deliberately not encoded as vectors here, because a rejection has no canonical signature to agree on.
